description: The ring's performance budget. Speed is a guardrail, not the point of the ring: each metric is an absolute ceiling that catches a gross regression (a per-event syscall, a lock on the hot path), not a comparison against an earlier build. Changing a ceiling is a reviewed change to this file, so 'within budget' always names a real, checkable number. scripts/check_perf_budget.sh enforces it in CI.

dispatch_overhead_ns.description: Per-event dispatch: producer enqueue, host route, subscriber dequeue, excluding work on the payload. Median over batched samples from c/bench/dispatch.c, 16-byte inline payload.
dispatch_overhead_ns.observed_note: measured when the benchmark lived in aimee (reference dev box). The ceiling carries ~7x headroom so CI variance does not flake the check while a per-event syscall still trips it.

dispatch_overhead_telemetry_ns.description: The same dispatch with D16 telemetry on: the host writes one record per event and a consumer thread drains them through the reader's paced wait, as an exporter would (OURO_BENCH_TELEMETRY=1).
dispatch_overhead_telemetry_ns.observed_note: measured 2026-10-31 on a Threadripper 3970X with both threads pinned to their own cores: 127 ns off, 132-133 ns on and paced (144-157 ns with pacing off). Same headroom rule as dispatch_overhead_ns.

telemetry_wakes.description: Doorbell writes during the telemetry-on run (telemetry_wakes=). A paced consumer kept busy is never asleep when a record lands, so the host rings it only for the first record; consumer pacing that stops working rings once per pump, about 8,000 times in this run. A count, not a time, so it means the same on every machine. The ceiling leaves room for a consumer descheduled past the idle threshold on a busy CI runner, which legitimately costs a wake, while staying 20x below what broken pacing produces.
